messages.subject: Observer variability
parts:
On Fri, 30 Jan 2004 08:37:32 -0700, Robin E Russell wrote:

> >Hi- I'm new to the list and I checked the archives but I didn't see this
> >question addressed directly, but I didn't want to send an irrelevant
> >message to several hundred people on first try. Anyway, my question is
> >regarding point count data. I have one particular observer who is
> >misjudging distances, however, I believe the problem is concentrated
> >between the first and second bins. (The bins are 0-10, 10-25, 25-50,
> >50-75, 75-100) Is there a problem with combining the first two bins to
> >compensate for this error? I know this means there will only be 4 bins and
> >therefore I may have problems with adjustment terms and lack of GOF tests.
> >I also know the new Distance book will discuss a methods of compensating if
> >you have some accurate estimates for the observer. In the meantime what do
> >you think of the above solution?

> >Thanks

> >Robin E. Russell

Hi Robin,

Seems like a reasonable question for archiving on the list, so I've forwarded
this message there.

There's no problem with combining the two bins -- indeed that's exactly what you
need to do in this case. However, it's probably going to have a bad effect on
the variance of the estimate of h(0) -- it will be harder for the fitting
algorithm to tell what the slope of the pdf is at 0 distance when it has such
large inner bins. No real alternative however.

You had the right approach in having two small inner bins, and increasing bin
width with distance from the point. Allows one more scope to test for problems
and look for a shoulder in the detection function.

I wouldn't worry too much about constraints on adjustment terms and GOF tests as
unless you have lots of data or a spiked detection function you're unlikely to
want lots of adjustment terms (a good general rule). Your main problem with GOF
tests will be lack of ability to look for a shoulder in the detection function.

Did you consider going to exact distances in future, or at least tightening up
on distance measurements using a laser rangefinder? For many point transect
studies, detections are mostly aural (of birds singing in forest, for example).
In reasonably open forest one may estimate distance by first guessing which
tree, bush, group of trees, etc the bird was singing from, and then estimating
the distance to that object. Laser rangefinders would remove the uncertainty
involved in the second part of this process. They may be of most use for the
closest birds detected, but then these are also the ones where you need the best
accuracy. Just a thought (may not be practical in your study) ...

- Len
